standard_text: Types of movement – amoeboid, ciliary, flagellar, muscular; skeletal muscle, contractile proteins and muscle contraction; skeletal system and its functions; joints; disorders of muscular and skeletal system – myasthenia gravis, tetany, muscular dystrophy, arthritis, osteoporosis, gout.

key_big: Thin (actin) filaments slide over thick (myosin) filaments.
body_html:
How to think about it

Cells move by amoeboid, ciliary, flagellar or muscular movement. A skeletal muscle fibre has myofibrils made of sarcomeres with thin actin and thick myosin filaments. A nerve impulse releases Ca²⁺, which binds troponin; myosin heads then pull actin inwards using ATP, shortening the sarcomere.

The adult skeleton has 206 bones: the axial skeleton (skull, vertebral column, sternum, ribs) and the appendicular skeleton (limbs and girdles). Joints may be fibrous, cartilaginous or synovial (ball and socket, hinge, pivot, gliding, saddle).

Example

Joint in the knee?

moves one way

Answer: hinge

Example

Ion that starts contraction?

binds troponin

Answer: Ca²⁺

Common mistakes

  • Saying the A-band shortens.
  • Calling the femur part of the axial skeleton.
  • Mixing up gout and osteoporosis.

faq.q: What is the sliding filament theory?
faq.a: Muscles contract as the thin actin filaments slide over the thick myosin filaments, shortening each sarcomere.

faq.q: How many bones are in the human skeleton?
faq.a: 206 in an adult: 80 in the axial skeleton and 126 in the appendicular skeleton.

items.q: What is osteoporosis?

loss of bone mass with age, often due to low oestrogen
inflammation of joints due to deposits of uric acid crystals
an autoimmune disorder affecting the neuromuscular junction
items.e: Osteoporosis: loss of bone mass with age, often due to low oestrogen.
